anti_generic_signature_read: Asked cold what an off-the-shelf version would not have: 'the piece's physical size is not decoration, it's the rank -- and the rank is the planet's real diameter. You do not need a reference card. You pick up two pieces, feel which is bigger, and you know which outranks which, and that answer is also astronomically true.' And second: 'Uranus's ring stands vertical while Saturn's lies near-horizontal. That is a real fact about the two planets, built into geometry rather than printed on a card.' In round 3 it chose between them for sealing: 'Seal the rings as the visible signature' -- the ladder being the better idea and the weaker sighting.
blind_action_read: 'A person sets up sixteen pieces on the grid, then picks a piece up by its base and places it on another square. That is the whole motion.' And on articulation: 'There are no hinges, axles, magnets, sliders or detents anywhere I can see. So: pieces translate across squares; nothing on the object articulates.'
blind_form_read: 'Each is two volumes: a low cylindrical puck base (all sixteen bases are the same diameter -- I checked this) and a sphere sitting on a short, narrower collar.' It separated relief from flat colour by its own test and got it right: the hoops and rings are relief because 'they break the sphere's silhouette'; the markings are flat because 'the sphere's silhouette stays a perfect circle straight through every marking, no marking casts a shadow or catches an edge highlight, and the colour boundaries have no bevel.' It measured the ladder's extremes: 'the largest ball is about twice the diameter of the smallest' -- against a sealed 26.97/13.78 = 1.96.
blind_held_read: Unprompted, before anything was revealed: 'It is a two-player abstract board game -- a boxed tabletop game with a tiled board, two opposed armies of sculpted spherical pieces on round pucks, and two moulded storage trays. If I saw it on a table I'd call it planet chess or solar-system checkers. Sixteen pieces, eight per side, each a small painted ball mounted on a low cylindrical base; the bases are white for one side and black for the other.' It read the trays correctly too: 'clearly the pieces' storage/reserve holders, one tray per army.'
blind_relationship_read: Four relationships, all reached blind: 'Two mirrored armies'; 'A true mirror, not a copy ... The two armies are chiral reflections of one another, not duplicates'; 'A size ranking ... the identical bases are what make the descent readable, because the only variable is the ball. Physical size IS the rank. And the order matches real planetary diameter'; and 'One tray per army, eight pockets each -- a one-to-one correspondence with the eight pieces.'
blind_subjects_read: All eight named cold, each with the cue recorded at the time: Jupiter from 'orange-and-cream horizontal bands plus a single dark red oval'; Saturn from its flat ring; Uranus from a 'featureless pale cyan sphere with a narrow ring standing nearly vertical ... Uranus is the tipped-over planet with a perpendicular ring plane'; Neptune from its dark spot; Earth -- 'I can read the shape of Africa at roughly (600,290)'; Venus, Mars and Mercury. It declined to guess on the board furniture it could not place: 'I have guesses but no cue strong enough to state one.'

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Asked cold in round 1, before the critic knew what the object was or that this was the decisive question: 'NO. Nothing at all. Confidence: very high -- as high as I can be from images.' It logged all eight close frames one by one, and on the four that look straight down the four poles of the two copies: 'the pole faces me directly and is bare ... No cap, no ring around the pole, no spot, no dot, no change of shade beyond the lighting falloff', and 'all four poles of both copies are presented face-on and centred, and all four are blank. If there were any polar treatment at all it would be unmissable in those frames. There is none.' It calibrated itself unprompted: 'the other pieces in this set clearly can carry surface markings ... So this is not a limitation of the rendering or the process.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NOTHING is drawn, painted, inlaid or marked on either Uranus globe -- no hood, no cap, no band, no spot, no stripe, no seam line, no pole marking, and no replacement in a quieter tone. The globe is one undivided `cyan` solid.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 2, fresh look: 'the band's upper section around (487,138) is near-white -- visually the brightest thing in frame apart from the base's lit top edge -- grading to mid-grey by (430,500) as it turns away from the light. That is a white material shaded, not a grey material.' The critic added its own honest limit: in the four polar frames the annulus renders mid-grey throughout, so white is verifiable from the hero and ring-plane frames and not from the polar ones.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Uranus carries a ring and the ring prints in `white`, the same filament Saturn's ring uses and the value `RING_COLOUR` holds as the set's default.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The critic corrected the Manager's wording here and then corroborated the object three ways. It rejected 'pole-over-pole' as describing a different and wrong thing: a complete concentric circle in the four polar frames puts the camera on the ring's axis, so the ring axis IS the polar axis and the hoop arches over the EQUATOR. It saw both attitudes in one frame: 'Upright hoop versus brim -- two completely different silhouettes, unmistakable side by side.' And it measured the lean from pixel endpoints it had written down in round 1 before any figure was given it -- '~490,140 down to ~420,640' -- computing 'atan(70/500) = 8.0 degrees from vertical, equal and opposite on the two copies' against the sealed 7.77.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The ring's geometry did not move. It is still an upright hoop standing on edge in Uranus's own equatorial plane -- which on a world tipped 97.77 degrees stands 7.77 degrees past vertical -- as against Saturn's ring, which lies in its own equatorial plane and so lies nearly flat. Same kind of part, two attitudes.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Discovered blind, unprompted, in round 1: 'Images 15 and 16 are the clincher: the cyan ball's hoop leans one way on the white-based piece (top of the hoop toward the right, ~490,140 down to ~420,640) and the opposite way on the black-based piece (top toward the left, ~410,140 down to ~480,640). The two armies are chiral reflections of one another, not duplicates.' Measured on the solids in `measure/uranus-mirror.md`: every body that must match matches to 0.0001 mm3.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The two Uranus pieces are exact mirrors of one another.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, unprompted: 'Four pieces, being two subjects, one in each army' and 'Can I tell the two subjects apart without being told? Yes, trivially, and I did before reading anything.' It ranked the cues itself: 'Colour. One is pale cream/yellow, the other is vivid cyan. This alone settles it at any distance', then 'Ring attitude. Horizontal brim vs upright band. This is the meaningful difference and it is visible even in the tiny board-distance renders.' And: 'Would I actually manage it across a table? Yes, easily ... This is the one piece of the design that works unambiguously at play distance.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: There are exactly two ringed worlds on the board and they are tellable apart from each other without being told which is which -- now that the ring's colour no longer helps, because both rings print `white`.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 2: 'Unambiguous in all eight close frames and both board frames ... It is the only cyan object in the set and the only piece I identified by colour alone.' In round 1 it named the world from that colour plus the ring attitude, cold.

Round 2, counted fresh on the pair frame: 'Three bands, roughly parallel, each closing round the globe. The dark oval sits at roughly (610,370) -- a clean grey-brown ellipse, fully on the globe, not clipped. Still present, still legible, unchanged.' In round 1, before disclosure, it had named the world from those cues.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Neptune still carries its three closed white latitude bands and its one dark oval spot, unchanged by this revision.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 2 -- and checking it made the critic withdraw two of its own round-1 defects. It had called the cap 'a blown-out white specular blob ... wiping out the band pattern'; on re-inspection: 'the cream and yellow bands run as concentric arcs around that white oval -- you can trace them curving round it at (605,175) and (700,285). Latitude bands do exactly that when the pole tips toward the camera. The white oval is the polar cap, correctly placed at the pole, and the banding around it is the proof.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Saturn still carries its five bands, its bright white northern cap and its flat white ring plate, unchanged by this revision.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, blind: 'Yes, the intent is unmistakably ordered -- a deliberate descending ladder, not an assortment.' It then claimed an inversion at one step and, shown the colour-segmented pixel widths of the exact frames it had been given, withdrew it and diagnosed its own error: 'my method carried an error band of at least 5-8 per cent per edge on a downscaled render, which is larger than the effect I claimed to detect ... Withdrawn.' It flagged the honest limit of its own sign-off: it can confirm five of the seven steps by eye and the two sub-0.2 mm steps pass on the measurement's authority, not on its own.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The eight globes of one army form a strictly ordered size ladder, largest to smallest, with no inversion at any step.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1: 'the only cues are (a) base colour, which works fine.' Round 2, asked whether the restatement had become trivially true, the critic said it had and argued for keeping it anyway: 'It is not vacuous. It can fail' -- its own defect 25, where the black base loses all readable form on this flat shader, is very nearly it failing, and colour survived where form did not -- and 'the load-bearing cue should be the trivial one. This is the discriminator a player uses on every single turn.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The two armies are told apart at play distance by the base, `white` against `black`.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 2, checked piece by piece across both ladder frames: 'banded orange world with red spot; pale banded world with polar cap and ring; blue world with three bands and oval; Earth with continents and caps; cream world with its swirl band; red world with pale patches; grey world with crater marks. Seven of eight carry markings. Exactly one globe is bare, and it is the cyan one.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NO world in the set other than Uranus is bare: nothing else lost a marking in this revision.

largest_risk: The critic's own words, sealed unedited: 'That it ends up owned rather than played. Every part of this object is finished to a standard that makes people want it on a shelf -- and rank, the one thing the game consists of, is the one thing the pieces will not tell you across a table. Two of the seven steps are a tenth of a millimetre, and the numeral that should rescue them cannot be read. The risk is not that someone dislikes it. It is that someone loves it, sets it up, gets four moves in, has to pick two pieces up and hold them together to find out which one wins, and quietly decides it is an ornament.' Neither half is in this revision's scope -- the ladder is frozen by the Wish and the numeral was not touched -- and both are recorded rather than answered. The second-largest risk is this revision's own and is in `resolution`.
resolution: Three review rounds, ZERO repairs, one independent critic, and NO geometry changed at any point: the images read blind in round 1 are the images sealed here. Round 1 was unprimed and identified the object, the two armies, the lift-and-place action and the mirror, named all eight worlds from cues, and answered this revision's decisive negative question without being told it was decisive. Of twenty-nine blind findings, thirteen were withdrawn on measurement -- twelve of them one error the critic diagnosed itself, reading an orthographic isometric view as if it had depth and turning projection overlaps into collisions -- seven were properties of a shadowless flat shader, nine stand as non-blocking, and NONE is blocking. Every self-quote attributed to an earlier round was checked against the transcript before sealing, in both directions: all verbatim or correctly elided, and the critic correctly refused to claim one phrase that was the Manager's. THE REVERSAL'S OWN COST, recorded rather than answered: asked cold whether any piece reads as a beach ball or a tennis ball, the critic named both Uranus pieces as BEACH BALLS at board distance -- 'a saturated, completely flat, glossy single-colour sphere with one bright white stripe running over it ... no surface detail whatsoever' -- while finding the reading dissolves close up into 'a ball in a standing hoop'. Told afterwards that the pale-panel half of the earlier reviewer's mechanism was gone, it did not move: 'The revision swapped one route to the toy-ball reading for another ... the second one is the one the revision built.' Its recommendation, for the owner to decide, is to leave the ring's filament alone and consider a darker tone of the globe's own cyan at the same 60-degree boundary. Nothing in this build acts on it: the ring is not changed back, no marking is added, nothing is tinted or softened. See measure/signature-review-protocol.md.
reviewer: One independent native critic, three rounds, shown only this build's twenty canonical renders. Round 1 was unprimed; rounds 2 and 3 are disclosed re-reviews on unchanged geometry.
